messages.content: You write the short explanations that first-year programming students in India type when a C quiz asks them "Why did you choose that answer?". Reply with a JSON object only.

A student was shown this C code and question.

Code:
int h(int n) { return h(n - 1); }

Question: What is h(2)?
The student answered: it never stops

The student understands this correctly: Recursion only stops at a base case that returns without calling itself; without one it never stops.

Write 5 different explanations this student might type for why they chose that answer.
Voice: long-winded, walks through the steps one by one, 20 to 35 words.

Rules:
- Each one must show the student's reasoning, not just repeat the answer.
- Write as the student, in the first person or with no subject. Do not judge the answer or say it is wrong.
- Do not name the idea as a rule and do not use textbook terms for the mistake.
- Make the 5 explanations differ in wording and in which part of the code they point at.

Return JSON: {"sentences": ["...", "..."]}

content: {"sentences": ["Starting h(2), it calls h(1), then h(0), then keeps going negative forever, because nothing inside ever returns a value without calling itself again.", "Look at the function body: there is only one line, and that line calls h again. So each call makes another call, endlessly, with no stopping point.", "When n equals 2, subtract 1 gives 1, then 0, then -1, and it never checks for a smallest number to quit at.", "The single return statement always contains another call to h, so there is no moment where execution can finish and hand a result back up.", "Every time h runs, it leaves a pending call and starts a new one, stacking up forever because no version just gives back a number."]}

sentences: Starting h(2), it calls h(1), then h(0), then keeps going negative forever, because nothing inside ever returns a value without calling itself again.
Look at the function body: there is only one line, and that line calls h again. So each call makes another call, endlessly, with no stopping point.
When n equals 2, subtract 1 gives 1, then 0, then -1, and it never checks for a smallest number to quit at.
The single return statement always contains another call to h, so there is no moment where execution can finish and hand a result back up.
Every time h runs, it leaves a pending call and starts a new one, stacking up forever because no version just gives back a number.
